newsitem.title: UK: Six die in Scottish food poisoning outbreak.
newsitem.headline: Six die in Scottish food poisoning outbreak.

text.p: Six elderly people have died of food poisoning in Scotland after eating suspect cooked meat and at least 107 are ill, health officials said on Wednesday.
A 69-year-old man and 79-year-old woman died early on Wednesday in a hospital in the southern Scottish town of Airdrie, a day after an 80-year-old man succumbed.
Three more elderly people died later on Wednesday, the Scottish Office said.
A spokeswoman for Law Hospital in Airdrie where the last victim died said 10 more people were also being treated there.
"We have six adults currently in hospital at the moment and four children suffering from the symptoms of food poisoning," she said. Two children were on kidney dialysis in one hospital.
Some victims had eaten steak pie from a local butcher's shop served at a pensioners' lunch 10 days ago.
The butchers had supplied cooked meat to more than 30 wholesale and retail food outlets in the region and officials urged people to avoid cooked meat form affected stores.
E coli is a common gut bacteria that is usually harmless, but some strains can cause poisoning.

The toxic strain normally lives in cattle but can be transmitted to humans through manure or improper slaughtering and can cause sudden kidney failure, permanent brain damage or death, especially in young children or the elderly.
Adults may suffer diarrhoea, stomach cramps or more mild, flulike symptoms after eating food tainted by the bacterium.
Health officials in Washington state, Colorado, California and Canada have reported more than 20 cases of food poisoning this month linked to E coli from unpasteurised apple juice.
In 1993, 500 people became ill in the Seattle area and three children died after eating undercooked hamburgers.
